content: Silicon dioxide, also known as silica or silox (derived from the Latin word silex), is a chemical compound composed of silicon and oxygen, with the chemical formula SiO₂. It has been recognized for its hardness since the 9th century. Silica is most commonly found in nature as sand or quartz and is also present in the cell walls of diatoms. It serves as a primary component in various materials, including glass and concrete. Silicon dioxide is widely used in the production of numerous products. For example, inexpensive soda-lime glass, which is commonly used in drinking glasses, bottles, and windows, is made from silica. It is also a raw material for manufacturing whiteware ceramics such as earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain, as well as for producing Portland cement. In the food industry, silica is used as a food additive, primarily as a flow agent in powdered foods or to absorb moisture. Additionally, the natural oxide coating that forms on silicon is highly beneficial in microelectronics due to its superior electrical insulation properties and high chemical stability. This oxide layer can protect silicon, store charge, block current, and act as a controlled pathway for small currents in electronic devices. However, at room temperature, the growth of this oxide layer is extremely slow, so thermal oxidation in high-temperature furnaces with an oxygen-rich environment is typically used to manufacture such layers. Silicon dioxide is also utilized in other applications, such as the production of aerogels for space exploration (e.g., in the Stardust spacecraft) and in the extraction of DNA and RNA, where it binds to nucleic acids in the presence of chaotropes. It is added to medicinal anti-foaming agents like simethicone to enhance defoaming activity and is used as hydrated silica in toothpaste to provide an abrasive action that helps remove plaque. Despite its many uses, prolonged inhalation of fine silica dust (e.g., concentrations above 1 mg/m³) can lead to serious health conditions such as silicosis, bronchitis, or, in rare cases, cancer. This occurs because the dust becomes lodged in the lungs, causing continuous irritation and reducing lung capacity, as silica does not dissolve over time. This occupational hazard is particularly relevant for individuals working with sandblasting equipment or products containing powdered silica. Vulnerable populations, such as children, asthmatics, allergy sufferers, and the elderly, may experience adverse effects in much shorter timeframes. However, in all other respects, silicon dioxide is chemically inert and harmless. When ingested orally, it passes unchanged through the gastrointestinal tract and is excreted in the feces without leaving any trace. Small pieces of silicon dioxide are also harmless as long as they are not large enough to obstruct the gastrointestinal tract or sharp enough to cause lacerations. Silicon dioxide does not produce fumes, is insoluble in vivo, and has no nutritional value or toxicity. Chemically, silicon dioxide forms when silicon is exposed to oxygen or air. A very thin layer of native oxide (approximately 1 nm thick) forms on the surface of silicon under ambient conditions. To grow well-controlled layers of silicon dioxide, higher temperatures and specific environments are used, such as dry or wet oxidation processes at temperatures between 600–1200°C using O₂ or H₂O, respectively. The thickness of the silicon replaced by the dioxide layer is approximately 44% of the thickness of the resulting silicon dioxide layer. Other methods for depositing SiO₂ include low-temperature oxidation of silane, decomposition of tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) at 680–730°C, and plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition using TEOS at around 400°C. Pyrogenic silica, also known as fumed silica, is a very fine particulate form of silicon dioxide prepared by burning SiCl₄ in an oxygen-rich hydrocarbon flame, producing a smoke of SiO₂. Quartz, a crystalline form of silicon dioxide, exhibits maximum solubility in water at around 340°C. This property is exploited in the hydrothermal process to grow single crystals of quartz, where natural quartz is dissolved in superheated water within a pressure vessel that is cooler at the top. Crystals weighing 5–1 kg can be grown over 1–2 months and are a source of very pure quartz for electronic applications. Fluorine reacts with silicon dioxide to form SiF₄ and O₂, while other halogen gases (Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) react much less readily. Silicon dioxide is attacked by hydrofluoric acid (HF) to produce hexafluorosilicic acid, and HF is commonly used in the semiconductor industry to remove or pattern silicon dioxide. In glass production, silicon dioxide is combined with other oxides (e.g., sodium oxide, potassium oxide, lead(II) oxide, zinc oxide) to form silicates and glasses, breaking the Si–O–Si bonds in silica. Examples include soda-lime glass, borosilicate glass, and lead glass, where silica acts as the network or lattice former. At high temperatures, silicon reacts to produce gaseous SiO. Structurally, silicon dioxide exists in several distinct crystalline forms in addition to amorphous forms. Most crystalline forms involve tetrahedral SiO₄ units linked by shared vertices in various arrangements, except for stishovite and fibrous sulfur. The Si–O–Si bond angle varies between 140° in α-tridymite and 180° in β-tridymite, with α-quartz having an angle of 144°. Fibrous sulfur has a structure similar to SiS₂, with chains of edge-sharing SiO₄ tetrahedra. Stishovite, the highest-pressure form, has a rutile-like structure where silicon is six-coordinated, resulting in a density of 4.287 g/cm³ compared to 2.648 g/cm³ for α-quartz. This density difference arises from the increased coordination and greater Si–O bond lengths in stishovite, which also increases the ionic character of the Si–O bond. Under normal conditions, α-quartz is the only stable form of crystalline silicon dioxide and is the most commonly encountered form. Impurities in α-quartz can give rise to various colors. Molecular forms of silicon dioxide, such as linear SiO₂, can be produced by condensing molecular silicon monoxide (SiO) in an argon matrix cooled with helium along with oxygen atoms generated by microwave discharge. Dimeric silicon dioxide (SiO₂)₂ has been prepared by reacting O₂ with matrix-isolated dimeric silicon monoxide (Si₂O₂).
